msItem.author: Isidore of Seville (d. 636), bishop of Seville
msItem.title: Etymologiae
msItem.note: CPL 1186; Bks I–X, ed. W. M. Lindsay (Oxford 1911); Díaz 122. Lindsay considered only early witnesses for his edition and did not notice ours. All twenty books are present here. Bk I is somewhat disordered, lacking c. 4 and positioning 3 before 16. Bk IV De medicina is miscalled Bk V in its rubric but not in the running head (41r). There seems to have been some sort of disruption in Bk X in the exemplar, perhaps holes or some other damage, for the scribe has here left empty lines as if seeing a lacuna. In fact, there is no text missing, as a later reader understood who drew connecting lines across the gaps. Greek words have been transliterated into Latin.

msItem.title: Sermo in festo S. Vincentii (serm. de sanctis 277A)

msItem.note: The remaining four lines of col. a are blank. A new hand, cursive minuscule of s. xiiex, has supplied in black ink in two columns the 95-year Alexandrian Easter table, separated as usual into five 19-year lunar cycles. The hand is that of the corrector, and the text was presumably taken from the copy that had supplied the corrected readings (see Annotations). It is significant that this text was transmitted with Isidore: for discussion, see I. Warntjes, ‘The continuation of the Alexandrian Easter table in seventh-century Iberia and its transmission to ninth-century Francia (Isidore, Etymologiae 6.17)’, Revue d’histoire des textes 13 (2018) 185–94.

Fol. 185 is blank but for ‘Passio: sectus ysaias . lapidatus erat Ieremias
Ezechia tractus . Amos per tempora fractus’ (s. xiv), upside down at the foot of the recto. It is worth the note that no mention of these martyrdoms is given in the Bible but they probably derive here instead from the pseudo-Epiphanian Liber de uitis prophetarum. (The martyrdoms of Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezechiel are also mentioned in that order in the long version of the apocryphal Visio Pauli, but not that of Amos.)

supportDesc.support: Parchment. Parchment is typical of Augustinian manuscripts: of even colour, smooth and pliant with a suede-like nap and an even sit, the leaves of varied thickness. There is little visual or tactile distinction between sides. Arranged like to like, hair-side outwards. There are quite a number of flaws in the parchment, for example holes around which the text was written (fols. 15, 17, 22, 38, 50, 51, 56, 57, 59, 63, 68, 72, 73, 98, 101, 113, 114, 141) and some inconspicuous natural edges (at fols. 17, 18, 26, 33, 34, 42, 73, 74, 84, 89, 113, 114, 117, 120, 125–128, 131, 132, 137, 139, 140, 142, 153, 156, 180). Some tears were once stitched but the thread has now gone: fols. 16, 19, 30, 32, 46, 51, 53, 59, 63, 68, 92, 98, 111, 112, 115, 128, 138, 143.
supportDesc.foliation: Foliated in early twentieth-century Bodleian pencil.
supportDesc.collation: 16 (fols. 1–5, first is pastedown) 2–158 (fols. 6–117) 1610 (fols. 118–127) 17–238 (fols. 128–183) 244 (fols. 184–185, first is a stub, fourth is pastedown). Catchwords are mostly ploughed away but exist at fols. 37v, 53v, 61v, 69v, 117v, 127v, 135v, 143v, 159v, 167v, 175v, while there are vestiges at 29v, 45v. They are written by a scribe who was not the main hand but was a close contemporary.

layoutDesc.layout: Ruled in lead for two columns of 37–42 lines with an intercolumnar space of 24 mm. Written above top-line. Vertical rules are single and pass to the edges. Horizontals are triples, sometimes quadruples at the top and bottom, of which only the two outer bounding lines pass to both edges, the others are extended to the outer edge only; in QQ6–8 there are also quadruples to the outer edge at the mid-point of the column. Lines cross the intercolumnar space. Pricked in both margins and ruled before folding. Prickings are mostly lost at the outer edge. Separate prickings for vertical rules.

handDesc.handNote: For the main text, two scribes writing fine romanesque bookhands of the mid-twelfth century. Scribe A is responsible for most of the book, going to fol. 137vb line 25. His hand shows a diminution of ascender height with a thick triangular serif and weighty dorsal fin to tall-s, as well as incipient lateral compression typical of the style. Except for majuscules, s is always tall, d is upright except for uncial d in combination with q in abbreviations of quid, quod, etc. A strictly controlled head- and base-line. Minims are finished with a consciously made turn of the nib. Ampersand only is used, also e-caudata, this latter having a sharply angular shape in the lower element that pushes out to the left. Insular abbreviation sign for est. A smaller-scale but otherwise identical script was used for the list of chapter headings at the start of each new book, set out catena-style, with much use of red and green for majuscules. The text ink is black. Punctuation is by low point for major medial pauses, and low point with following majuscule for sentences; punctus interrogativus is found, imperceptible from punctus elevatus, which is used for minor pauses. The scribe was a most careful copyist and any corrections have been made invisibly; omissions of more than a few words are visible where the correction has been made smaller to fit, and the overwriting is here on a washed rather than scraped surface, as at 16rb, 101vb, 108vb. The text script becomes smaller from fol. 70r, the start of a new quire, the ink browner at this point.

Scribe B writes from fol. 137vb line 26 to the end of the main text, 182vb, l. 16. The hand is very similar to Scribe A’s but slightly less consistent, with wavering minims and a less firmly controlled headline. The lower bowl of g swings out diagonally to terminate in front of the upper bowl and comes to a point with a sharp hairline that closes the bowl. Use of ampersand only. Chapter headings listed at the start of a new book are given in a script that is only slightly smaller than text size and tabulated, with green, red and blue majuscules.

A third scribe copied the two sermons on St Vincent at the end, beginning on fol. 182vb, l. 17. Again, it is a fine romanesque bookhand similar to Scribe A’s but closer to the third quarter of the twelfth century. It is notable for its use of uncrossed Tironian nota for et alongside ampersand. Round-s is routine in terminal position; uncial d is occasionally found in initial position and nearly always in q-abbreviations.

Much use of rubrication for chapter headings, done throughout the main text by the Scribe A, who also supplied the rubricated running headings. These take the form of ‘liber’ on the verso and a roman ordinal on the recto (jus, ijus, etc.). Chapter headings (but not the running headings) are missing for Bk X, only chapter numbers are marked (fols. 91r–98r). This is the part of the text where there seems to have been damage in the exemplar and the scribe left space, seeing lacunae. For the two sermons on St Vincent at the back of the volume, tituli are given in text ink and then lined through in red; there are no running headings.

decoDesc.decoNote: Handsomely decorated by the same hand throughout in a bright palette of red, blue, and acid green. The major initial at the start of the text proper, on fol. 6r, is an eight-line initial D of blue ink with a patterned stem of three green panels outlined in yellow. Infill of scrolling acanthus stems left in reserve on a blue, green and red ground with an opening acanthus bud at the head and foot of the stem. Other large initials stand at the start of the table and the head of each book (2v, 21v, 32r, 41r, 45v, 54r, 63r, 73v, 81v, 91r, 98r, 105r, 116v, 122v, 131r, 139r, 149v, 160v, 167r, 177v). These are of five to nine lines and done in the three colours, with attractive symmetrical motifs such as clove curls unfolding to release a split petal or three-lobed bud. There are geometrical patterns in the bodies of the letters or else they are given special treatment and parted in two colours, as the initial R at 21v, A at 167r, and P at 177v; this last initial is made especially fine.
Minor initials for chapters are two- or three-line lombards in one colour, standing out into the margin, often with arabesques in a contrasting colour.

Alexander & Temple gave the manuscript’s place of production as Durham, seeing a relation to the style of decoration used in the Benedictine cathedral priory there. The suggestion is not particularly compelling: the decoration uses a palette of colours and range of motifs that resemble much more closely those in Augustinian manuscripts than they do manuscripts from Durham. Those northern Augustinian initials were influenced by Cistercian books, but are more flamboyantly colourful. An origin among Augustinian canons also aligns better with the manuscript’s later provenance at Worksop.

additions.p: Over the start of the text on fol. 6r, one hand of s. xv wrote ‘liber Ysiod’ Ehimolog’ ’ in the top left corner and ‘Ysiodorus Ethimolog’’ at the top right. Throughout, there is the hand of a later twelfth-century corrector, who used a black ink and wrote an upright cursive minuscule. His annotations are in the range of verbal corrections, interlineated above the word which was struck through, or added on the line in the adjacent margin, sometimes connecting to the word with the sign of a double virgule. He also added the Alexandrian Easter table to blank space after the end of the text, derived presumably from the same exemplar used for the corrections since it is a text transmitted with Isidore. There are manicules at 4r, v, both pointing to passages in the opening epistles about divine love, for which all things are to be done (4r) and from which it is wrong to withdraw (4v).

The principal annotator was Robert Flemming. Specimens of his mature hand cluster thickly in the central portion of the manuscript, Bks VIII–XI (concerning respectively ‘De ecclesia et synagoga’, ‘De linguis gentium’, ‘Origo quorundam nominum’, and ‘De homine et partibus eius’). This was the part of the work that provided him with the richest mine of classical names: he wrote them in the margin next to their occurrence in the text. At the foot of 86r, under the start of IX 3 ‘De regno et regibus’, he repeated from the text ‘Regie virtutes Iustitia & pietas’; the definition of secular power is a familiar concern for him.

binding.p: A medieval binding, perhaps fourteenth-century, of whittawed skin over oak boards, cushion bevelled and flush to the text-block at head and tail with a deep overhang at the fore-edge. The boards seem older and to have been reused, since both show beneath the pastedowns longer, straight lacing paths in which the thongs are still present. The present arrangement is of V-lacing, likewise visible under both pastedowns. The leather of the covering is scuffed and small patches are rubbed away on both boards with a larger loss at the top corner of the upper board, which has revealed the housing of the fore-edge strap. Sewn on six double whittawed leather thongs, raised at the spine. There are tying-up marks on the covering of both boards. Endbands are structural and of blue and white thread around an alum-tawed leather core. There is secondary sewing through the spine of both head- and tailcaps; the former begins with red thread. Edges are stained red. Paired fore-edge clasps were leather straps which have been cut off flush to the board; their stubs are still in situ in grooves in the upper board, covered with leather and secured with three nails. The catch-plates are still in place on the lower board. Rust marks on fols. 1–3 may show the marks of another former clasp: they come at mid-point at the fore-edge. Probably belonging to the book’s time at Worksop, the marks left by an iron chain-staple are near the foot of the front board at the fore-edge: the extent of the plate was 14 × 35 mm and it was fixed by two nails. Nail holes and verdigris marks from the early-modern brass chain-clip are in the usual position towards the head of the fore-edge on the lower board. The location of the former title-piece is shown by six nail holes on the back board, two rows of three. The space bounded by the nail holes is 22 × 115 mm. The label survives and is now pasted to fol. 5v, below the inscription recording the book’s loan to Robert Flemming (see Labels and Marks). Pastedowns, thick leaves of medieval parchment, are original. The one at the back is half lifted, the one at the front is a half-leaf; where each board is visible it shows a light brown layer of dried paste. On the front pastedown is written ‘Ehtimologia (sic) ysidori’ (s. xiii), and beneath that an ex libris for Worksop priory (s. xvmed).).

history.provenance: The list of archbishops of Canterbury that was added to fol. 1r offers some dating evidence in that the final entry is for William of Corbeil, who died on 2 November 1136. His successor, Theodore of Bec, was elected 24 December 1138, consecrated 8 January 1139, and died 18 April 1161. This flyleaf is an integral part of the first quire, so the list was evidently added to a book which had been written before April 1161. It is not impossible that it was written after William’s death and before Theodore’s election at the end of 1138, but decoration and script would suggest a date nearer the middle of the century. The place of origin is not known, but decoration and parchment preparation point to a house of Augustinian canons. The earliest evidence for provenance is indeed Augustinian, provided by mid-fifteenth-century inscriptions for the priory of St Mary the Virgin and St Cuthbert at Worksop (Notts). In the same hand are: ‘¶ Constat Mon’ de Wyrkesopp’’ (front pastedown) and ‘¶ De Wyrkesopp’ liber iste’ (much faded at the foot of fol. 6r, the first leaf of text).

In the same stylish hand is the longer inscription on fol. 5v, facing the start of the text: 'Iste Liber Constat Monasterio beate Marie Sanctique Cuthberti Canonic’ Regular’ | de Wyrkesopp’ in Comitatu Not’ iuxta Schyrewod’ deliberat’ Magistro | Roberto Flemmyng’ Decano Ecclesie Cathedralis Lyncoln’; ex comodato et precario | per Manus Magistri Caroli Flemmyng’ Prioris eiusdem Anno Domini M°.CCCC°. lvij°.’ The inscription records the chapter’s decision in 1457 to put the book into Charles Flemming’s hands for delivery to Robert Flemming. Charles Flemming, of aristocratic birth and undoubtedly a kinsman to Richard and Robert, was, like them, a graduate of Oxford, admitted Bachelor of Canon Law in 1449. By 9 March 1451 he was prior of Worksop and remained so until his resignation on 8 October 1463, after which he disappears from the record (Heads, 3. 555; BRUO 696). In 1457 when this manuscript was entrusted to Charles, Robert had long been in Rome, originally as king’s proctor at the curia and then as apostolic protonotary. On 28 September 1458 Charles received special licence to visit Rome, which would have afforded him the opportunity to greet his kinsman and to hand him this manuscript. His presence there is unexplained, but the volume would have been a boon for eliciting Robert’s assistance at the curia, were that the reason for the visit.

It is also the case that Robert Flemming was experienced in soliciting loans. In 1453 he borrowed a twelfth-century Byzantine copy of Basil the Great’s Liturgy from Darley abbey (Derbys), which is now Bodl. MS Laud Gr. 28 (SC 705). Its inscription is reminiscent of the one in our manuscript: ‘Iste liber est de Abbathia de Derley accomodatus venerabili viro magistro Roberto Flemmyng decano Lyncolnie in vigilia Epiphenie anno domini Mo cccco lijo’ (fol. 1v). Flemming made no annotations in this Darley manuscript, and its later history outside of Lincoln College suggests that he had duly returned the book. (There are inscriptions for churchmen in Derby but these seem to be earlier than the Flemming inscription.) Unlike the Darley book, our manuscript entered Flemming’s own collection and came to the College after his death in 1483. The question then falls as to whether the transaction with Worksop involved a tacit understanding that Robert might keep the volume, or whether instead it was found among his effects after his death and was mistakenly bundled up with the books that passed to the College.

Labels and marks. Ownership marks for the Augustinian priory of St Mary the Virgin and St Cuthbert at Worksop (Notts) are on the front pastedown and fol. 6r. There is a long inscription recording the book’s loan to Robert Flemming (5v) and beneath this the College’s medieval title label from the back cover has been pasted. Measuring 15 × 97 mm, in the usual Textura hand it reads, ‘Ysidorus ethi’ ex dono Magistri Roberti | Flemmyng Decani Lincoln’’. There is no James number, but there is the mark (like an arabic nine with an oblique line rising to the right from the tail) over the start of the text (2v) as in other books which this Oxford reader could not find in the Ecloga. The brown-ink seventeenth-century pressmark is at the top of fol. 2r: ‘ff.: 51: 13’. The College bookplate of 1703 is affixed in normal position at the centre of the front pastedown. Beneath it is written the modern shelf-mark in purple crayon: ‘Linc. Coll. MS 63’, against which in pencil is ‘Lat (c)’. On the spine, two square paper labels: at the head, the arabic numeral 29 on the small, square printed label; at the foot, the printed label with modern shelf-mark, ‘MS. Linc. Coll. [[c.]] Lat. 63’. Vestiges of the fore-edge label are present, pasted to the wood where the leather is lost, but there is nothing legible.
history.acquisition: Acquired with the collection of Robert Flemming after his death in 1483.
